primer.body: Partners sit opposite each other. A 52-card deck is dealt evenly, giving every player 13 cards. North-South compete against East-West.
primer.title: Four players, two partnerships

primer.body: Each player contributes one card. You must follow the suit led when you can. The highest card in that suit wins unless a trump is played.
primer.tip: The trick winner leads the next trick.
primer.title: Win tricks

primer.body: Before play, the auction sets a target. A bid names a level from 1 to 7 and a suit or notrump. The level is how many tricks above six your side promises.
primer.tip: A contract of 4♠ promises 10 tricks with spades as trump.
primer.title: Bid a contract

primer.body: High-card points help describe a hand: ace 4, king 3, queen 2, jack 1. In Standard American, pass below 13 points and open one of a suit with 13 or more (a good 12 can open by the Rule of 20).
primer.tip: A balanced 15 to 17 HCP hand usually opens 1NT.
primer.title: Count your strength

primer.body: In the winning partnership, the player who first named the contract's denomination becomes declarer. Their partner lays dummy face up after the opening lead. The other partnership defends.
primer.tip: Declarer chooses every card played from dummy.
primer.title: Declarer, dummy, defenders

primer.body: That is the shape of bridge: describe the hand, choose a contract, then plan and play 13 tricks. Each room builds one skill in a few focused minutes.
primer.title: You're ready to train

items.backBody: Spades and hearts are the major suits. Diamonds and clubs are the minor suits. A standard bridge deck has 13 cards in each suit.
Within a suit, cards rank A, K, Q, J, 10 down to 2. The ace is normally the highest card.
Ace = 4 points, king = 3, queen = 2, jack = 1. Add those values across your 13 cards to estimate your hand's strength.
Each player contributes one card. The highest card of the suit led wins unless a trump is played. The trick winner leads next.
If you hold a card in the suit led, you must play one. Only when you are void in that suit may you discard or play a trump.
A contract level counts tricks above the first six. Four means 6 + 4 = 10 tricks. The denomination names trump, or NT when there is no trump.
items.backTitle: Ten tricks with spades as trump

items.backBody: Declarer plays the contract. Declarer's partner becomes dummy after the opening lead, lays all 13 cards face up, and plays the cards declarer calls.

items.explanation: Book is the first six tricks. Contract levels name the number of tricks required beyond book.
items.prompt: What does bridge players' word “book” mean?

items.explanation: 3NT is game. The other common game levels are 4♥, 4♠, 5♣, and 5♦.
items.prompt: Which is a game contract?

items.explanation: A level-six contract requires 6 + 6 = 12 tricks. Level seven is a grand slam requiring all 13.
items.prompt: How many tricks does a small slam require?

items.explanation: Dummy lays the hand face up and takes no part in the play. Declarer names each card to be played from it.

choices: Whenever you want to win the trick
Only when you are void in the suit led

items.backBody: In Standard American (SAYC), open one of a suit with 13 or more points and pass with fewer. A 12 may open by the Rule of 20: add your points to the lengths of your two longest suits, and open if the total is 20 or more.
Open 1NT with 15 to 17 high-card points and a balanced hand. Balanced means no singleton or void and at most one doubleton: 4-3-3-3, 4-4-3-2 or 5-3-3-2.

With opening strength and a five-card major, open that major. The exception is a balanced 15 to 17, which Standard American (SAYC) opens 1NT even with a five-card suit. A minor of six or more cards is longer, so you open that first.
With opening strength but no five-card major, open your longer minor. With three clubs and three diamonds, open 1♣. With four of each, open 1♦.

After partner opens, count your points and support. In Standard American, pass with 0 to 5, respond with 6 or more, and think of 6 to 9 as minimum, 10 to 12 as an invitation to game, and 13 or more as game strength.
items.backTitle: Place your hand in a range

items.explanation: This hand has 6 HCP: Q=2, K=3, and J=1. It is well below the 13 you need to open, so pass.
This hand has 14 HCP and five spades. Open the five-card major, 1♠.
With 14 HCP and five hearts, open 1♥.
This balanced hand has 16 HCP, right in the 15 to 17 range. Open 1NT.
This balanced hand has 16 HCP, so open the descriptive 1NT rather than a minor.
This hand has opening strength, five diamonds, and no five-card major. Open the longer minor, 1♦.
This balanced hand has 16 HCP. The 1NT range takes priority over choosing between the minors.

drills.title: Name Your Opening

items.explanation: Six spades and 13 HCP make 1♠ the clear opening.
This hand has 14 HCP, five clubs, and no five-card major. That is too weak for 1NT, which needs 15 to 17, so open your longer minor, 1♣.
The five-card heart suit and opening strength point to 1♥.
Six high-card points and no long suit. You need 13 to open at the one level, so pass.
Fifteen points, balanced 4-3-3-3, and no five-card major. That is the 1NT range exactly.
Thirteen points and no five-card major, but too weak for 1NT. Open your longer minor, 1♦.
Thirteen points with a six-card heart suit. Open the major and tell partner about the length straight away.

items.backBody: In notrump, count tricks you can take without giving up the lead. Then identify the suit that can produce the extra tricks you need.
If your plan does not depend on ruffing losers in the short-trump hand, draw opponents' trumps so they cannot ruff your winners.
items.backTitle: When opponents' trumps are the danger

items.backBody: The ace may take the first round, but your remaining honors can become winners. Giving up one trick can create several later.
Lead toward the A-Q. If the next defender plays low, play the queen. It wins when the missing king sits with the defender who plays before the A-Q hand.
items.backTitle: Play for a missing honor to be well placed

items.backBody: Playing low in second seat often preserves your honor to capture a later card. It is a guideline, not a rule, but a strong default.

drills.subtitle: Flashcards: winners, trump, finesses, and timing
drills.title: Declarer Playbook

items.reasoning: You hold a heart, so you must follow suit with the 2♥.
items.situation: West leads the 7♥. You hold these four cards. Which card is legal?
items.tip: Following suit is mandatory. Winning the trick is not.

items.reasoning: The 10♣ beats the 9♣. Save the king and ace for later tricks.
items.situation: You are declarer in notrump. West leads 4♣, dummy plays 6♣, and East plays 9♣. You play last. Which card wins most cheaply?
items.tip: Win with the lowest card that does the job.

items.reasoning: Because you are void in spades, you may play a trump. Even the 2♥ beats every non-trump card in the trick.
items.situation: Hearts are trump. A spade is led and you have no spades. Which card can win the trick?
items.tip: A low trump outranks a high card in the suit led.

items.reasoning: The ace is the only card here that beats the king. Play A♦ to win the trick.
items.situation: No trump is in play. You are last to a trick of 10♦, 3♦, K♦. Which card wins?
items.tip: Compare only cards in the suit led when there is no trump.

items.reasoning: Any card is legal when you cannot follow suit. Throw the card you need least, here the 2♦, and keep your ace and king.
items.situation: Clubs are led in notrump and you have no clubs. Any card is legal. Which is the sensible discard?
items.tip: A discard cannot win unless it is trump, and notrump has no trump suit.

drills.subtitle: Table situations: make the legal, winning play
drills.title: Choose the Card

items.reasoning: Play K♦. Covering may promote partner's jack or ten into a winner.
items.situation: Declarer leads Q♦ toward dummy. You hold K♦ and play second. Which card follows the guideline “cover an honor with an honor”?
items.tip: The guideline is strongest when partner may hold the next lower honor.

items.reasoning: Play low. If you rise with the king, dummy's ace wins and the jack may become good.
items.situation: Declarer leads 4♣ from hand. You hold K-8-2 and play second, with dummy's A-J behind you. What is the usual play?
items.tip: Second hand low protects honors that sit in front of dummy.

items.reasoning: Play Q♠ because it is your only spade. It also unblocks the suit so partner can continue cleanly.
items.situation: Partner leads A♠ from A-K. You hold a singleton queen. Which card must you play?
items.tip: Following suit comes before every defensive signal.

items.reasoning: Start drawing trumps with a high trump, here the ace. Leaving the defenders' trumps outstanding invites one of them to ruff a winner of yours.
items.situation: You are in 4♠ with no side-suit shortness, and the defenders still hold trumps. What do you usually lead first?
items.tip: Delay drawing trumps only when you need dummy's trumps for ruffing first.

items.reasoning: An ace cannot be beaten, so it is a sure winner. A queen or a small card only wins once the higher cards in its suit are gone, so you cannot count it yet.
items.situation: In a notrump contract you count your sure winners before playing to trick one. Which of these cards is a sure winner when led?
items.tip: In notrump count winners. In a suit contract count losers.

items.reasoning: Protect the outside ace. Without an entry the established clubs are unreachable and the whole plan collapses.
items.situation: Dummy holds a long solid club suit but only one outside entry. Which card do you protect?
items.tip: A long suit is worth nothing if you cannot get to it.

items.reasoning: Ruff with a trump. Dummy is out of diamonds, so a loser in your hand becomes a trick in dummy, as long as no defender can overruff.
items.situation: You are in 4♥ and lead a losing diamond from your hand. Dummy has no diamonds but still has trumps. Which dummy card do you play?
items.tip: Ruff in the hand with the fewer trumps, so you keep enough to draw the opponents'.

rooms.tagline: Plan the hand and choose the card

items.backBody: From a solid sequence, lead the top card. The king tells partner you hold the touching honors below it.
items.frontSubtitle: Lead the K♠ or a low spade?

items.backBody: Against notrump, a long suit is your best chance to establish extra tricks. Without a sequence, lead a low card.
An unsupported ace is often more valuable as an entry or capture later. Do not automatically cash aces on opening lead.
When partner leads and dummy plays low, third hand often plays high to force out declarer's higher card or win the trick.
Partner chose that suit for a reason. Returning it helps establish and cash the partnership's winners.

drills.subtitle: Make the call, then flip for the coach's answer
drills.title: Lead or Hold?

items.explanation: Without a strong sequence, lead fourth best from the top: the four. It tells partner about your length as well as your suit.
items.prompt: Against notrump you lead your longest suit. From K-9-7-4-2, which card is the standard lead?

items.explanation: Partner told you where their strength is. Leading their suit is usually the friendliest start, unless you have a strong reason of your own.
items.prompt: Partner overcalled hearts during the auction. What is a reasonable opening lead?

items.explanation: Third hand high. You are trying to win the trick or force out a high card, since dummy has already passed on it.
items.prompt: Partner leads a small card and dummy plays low. As third hand, what is the general rule?

choices: It gives up control and may set up declarer's king
Aces cannot be led at trick one
items.explanation: An ace with no king behind it usually wins only small cards, and it can turn declarer's king into a winner. Save the ace to capture an honor.
items.prompt: Why is leading an unsupported ace against a suit contract usually a poor choice?

choices: Playing cards in an order that shows how many you hold
items.explanation: Playing high then low usually shows an even number of cards, low then high an odd number. Partnerships agree on this in advance.
items.prompt: What does it mean to give partner count?

items.backBody: Lead the top of a touching honor sequence. It describes the holding and avoids giving away a cheap trick.
A trump lead can remove dummy's ruffing power and cut down declarer's crossruff.
A singleton can create a ruff when partner gets the lead and returns the suit.
This is an interior sequence. The jack is safe, describes the holding to partner, and keeps the king guarding the suit.
Top of a doubleton. Following with the three next time shows partner the suit was two cards long and may set up a ruff.
Leading through dummy's honors means declarer has to commit before partner plays. The old phrase is lead through strength, up to weakness.
items.frontTitle: Dummy's strength sits on your left

items.backBody: When the opponents have only just enough strength, they often need you to help. A quiet lead avoids handing over the one trick they were missing.
items.frontTitle: The opponents stretched to a thin game

items.backBody: A high spot card is the standard encouraging signal. Partnerships vary, so agree your discard method before you sit down.
items.frontTitle: You must discard and want a diamond back

items.explanation: A takeout double shows support for the unbid suits and asks partner to choose one, unless partner has a special reason to pass.
items.prompt: Left-hand opponent opens 1♥. A takeout double usually asks partner to do what?

choices: Describe a long suit and consume bidding space
items.explanation: A preempt shows a long suit and limited hand while making the opponents start their exchange at a higher level.
items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a preemptive opening?

items.explanation: Stayman asks the 1NT opener whether they hold a four-card major.
items.prompt: After partner opens 1NT, what does 2♣ Stayman ask?

items.explanation: Transfers place the strong 1NT hand as declarer, keeping its honors concealed on opening lead.
items.prompt: After 1NT, a Jacoby transfer primarily lets which hand become declarer?

items.reasoning: Play Q♥. It wins when the missing king is with the opponent who already played.
items.situation: You lead low toward A-Q of hearts. Left-hand opponent follows low. Which card executes the finesse?
items.tip: The ace remains as a later winner and entry.

items.reasoning: Duck a small card early. Winning the ace immediately may let defenders run the suit when they regain the lead.
items.situation: In 3NT, opponents lead a suit where you hold A-3-2 and dummy has two small cards. Which card do you play on the first round to break their communication?
items.tip: Count the suit before holding up. Do not duck if the contract is in immediate danger elsewhere.

items.reasoning: Play the nine. It loses at most one trick to the queen or ten, and your ace, king and jack stay in reserve. Cashing the ace or king first can leave East with queen-ten behind your jack and cost you two tricks.
items.situation: You need three club tricks from A-K-J-9 in your hand and 5-4-3 in dummy. The queen and ten could both be with East. You lead the 5♣ from dummy and East plays low. Which club do you play from your hand?
items.tip: A safety play trades the maximum result for a better chance to make the contract.

choices: How your result compares with other pairs
items.explanation: Duplicate matchpoints compare your score on a board with every pair holding the same direction.
items.prompt: At matchpoints, what matters most?

items.explanation: Four of a major is the lowest game level, worth 120 trick points. Higher contracts also score game but need more tricks.
items.prompt: What is the lowest major-suit contract that earns the game bonus?

items.explanation: Vulnerability increases the game bonus and the penalties for going down.
items.prompt: Vulnerability changes which two things most directly?

items.explanation: The eight is your highest spare card and reads as encouraging. The queen is too valuable to throw and the four discourages.
items.prompt: Partner leads the ace and you hold Q-8-4. Playing standard signals, which card encourages a continuation?

choices: Your highest card in the ruffed suit
Your lowest card in the ruffed suit
items.explanation: Suit preference: a high card asks for the higher-ranking side suit, a low card for the lower. It is one of the most useful agreements in defense.
items.prompt: You are giving partner a ruff and want them to return the higher of the two remaining side suits. What do you lead for the ruff?

choices: Ruffing high to force declarer to overruff with an honor
Leading a trump at trick one
items.explanation: Ruffing with a card declarer must beat can promote a trump trick for partner. Losing your ruff to gain a bigger trick is the whole idea.
items.prompt: What is an uppercut in defense?

items.explanation: The discard shows exactly two clubs. Thirteen cards total: 5 + 4 + 2 leaves 2 diamonds. Counting the hand out is what separates good defenders from lucky ones.
items.prompt: Declarer has shown five spades and four hearts, followed to two rounds of clubs, then discarded on the third round. How many diamonds do they hold?

choices: When playing low would let a singleton or doubleton honor in dummy win
items.explanation: Rules of thumb bend to the layout. If ducking hands declarer a trick they could not otherwise take, rise instead.
items.prompt: When is second hand high right rather than second hand low?
